title: From DNA to Protein: The Central Dogma
hook: Your DNA is a recipe book locked in the nucleus — so the cell copies a single recipe to RNA, carries it out, and reads it to build a protein.
key_points: The central dogma describes information flowing from DNA to RNA to protein.
Transcription copies a gene's DNA into a messenger RNA (mRNA).
Translation reads the mRNA in three-letter codons to assemble a protein.
Proteins do most of the work in cells, so this is how genes shape traits.
content_html: DNA holds the instructions for building you, but those instructions have to be read and acted on. Biologists summarize the flow of that information as the central dogma: DNA to RNA to protein. The cell never sends the master DNA out to do the work; instead it makes a disposable copy, carries it out, and uses it as a build sheet.
extra_html: It happens in two steps. First, transcription copies a single gene from DNA into a strand of messenger RNA (mRNA) — like photocopying one recipe rather than carrying the whole cookbook around. Then, in translation, a ribosome reads the mRNA three bases at a time. Each three-letter group, called a codon, names a specific amino acid, and the ribosome links those amino acids into a chain that folds into a protein. As Khan Academy lays out, this pathway matters because proteins do most of the actual work in a cell — so transcription and translation are how the information in your genes becomes real traits.

related.title: What Is DNA?
related.hook: A four-letter chemical code, coiled into a double helix, carries the full instruction manual for building and running a living thing.

related.title: How Genes Become Traits
related.hook: You inherit two copies of every gene — one from each parent — and the way those copies interact helps decide everything from eye color to blood type.

related.title: Mutations: When DNA Changes
related.hook: Every time a cell copies its DNA, tiny typos can slip in — most do nothing at all, a few cause disease, and rare ones fuel evolution.

flashcards.prompt: What is the 'central dogma' of molecular biology?
flashcards.back_html: The flow of genetic information: DNA → RNA → protein. DNA is transcribed into RNA, and RNA is translated into protein.

choices.text: A gene's DNA is copied into messenger RNA
A protein is broken down into amino acids

flashcards.explanation_html: In transcription, the cell makes an RNA copy (mRNA) of a gene's DNA sequence, which can then leave the nucleus to be read.

flashcards.prompt: During translation, the mRNA is read in units of how many bases?
flashcards.explanation_html: mRNA is read in three-base groups called codons, and each codon specifies a particular amino acid to add to the growing protein.
